title: Addition in any order
keyIdea: You can add two numbers in any order and get the same total: 3 + 8 = 11 and 8 + 3 = 11. So when you count on, start on the bigger number and count on the smaller one. Take-away is different: 5 − 3 = 2, but you cannot take 5 away from 3, so a take-away does not turn round.

kid: Look at a domino with 3 dots and 8 dots. 3 and 8 make 11. Now turn it round. It is 8 and 3. The dots did not change, so it still makes 11.
That means you can pick the order. For 2 + 9, start on 9. Then count on just 2: 10, 11. That is much quicker than 9 hops from 2.

Each sum has a turnaround buddy. 4 + 7 turns round to 7 + 4. Keep both numbers and swap them. The total stays the same. With three numbers, add the easy two first. For 7 + 5 + 3, do 7 + 3 = 10. Then 10 + 5 = 15.
Take-away does not turn round. You can take 3 away from 5 and have 2 left. Try to take 5 away from 3. You run out!
adult: This is the commutative property of addition: a + b = b + a. The US Common Core asks Grade 1 children to 'apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract', with the examples 'if 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known' (commutative) and '2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12' (associative) (1.OA.3). The English national curriculum asks Year 2 pupils to 'show that addition of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction of one number from another cannot'.

The practical pay-off is choosing the order that is easiest. Counting on from the larger addend (researchers call it the 'min' strategy, because the child counts on the smaller number) roughly halves the facts a child needs to learn and cuts the counting: 2 + 9 becomes two hops from 9 rather than nine hops from 2. With three numbers, children can add any two first, so they look for a pair that makes 10, a number bond they already know. The total never changes; only the effort does.

Common mistakes to watch for: believing that 8 + 3 needs working out again after 3 + 8; always starting on the first number written, even when it is small; carrying the idea over to subtraction and saying 3 − 5 = 2; writing the digits side by side, so 8 + 3 becomes 83; and counting the start number as a hop. Ask 'did the dots change?' when a child turns a sum round, and 'can you take 5 counters from 3?' when they swap a take-away. Negative numbers come much later, so for now 3 − 5 simply cannot be done with counters.

In the lab your child turns dominoes round, chooses the bigger number to count on from, finds the turnaround card for a sum (and turns down a take-away decoy), takes counters away both ways round, and adds three numbers by making 10 first.

familyTip: Use a handful of buttons or pasta. Put 2 in one hand and 6 in the other, and ask how many there are. Then swap your hands round and ask again. Does it change? Next, show 6 and ask your child to take away 2, then hand them 2 and ask them to take away 6.

visual.caption: Do the two sides give the same answer? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: turn dominoes round, start on the bigger number, find turnaround facts, try take-aways both ways and make 10 first.

practice.hint: Turning a sum round does not change the total. The numbers are the same, just swapped.
practice.explain: {b} + {a} uses the same two numbers as {a} + {b}, so it is {=a+b} too.

practice.prompt: {a} + {b}. Start on {b} and count on. How many hops do you make?
practice.hint: Start on the bigger number, {b}. Count on the smaller number, one hop at a time.
practice.explain: Start on {b} and hop {a} times to land on {=a+b}. That is only {a} hops, not {b}.

practice.prompt: Which sum is the same as 4 + 7 turned round?
practice.hint: Keep both numbers. Just swap their places.
practice.explain: 7 + 4 is 4 + 7 turned round. Both make 11. 7 − 4 is a take-away, and 4 + 4 changes a number.

choices: No, take-away does not turn round
practice.hint: Can you take 6 counters away if you only have 2?
practice.explain: No. 6 − 2 = 4, but you cannot take 6 away from 2. Adding turns round; take-away does not.

pool.prompt: Work out {a} + {b}. Tip: start on the bigger number.
pool.hint: Start on {b}, then count on {a} more.
pool.explain: Start on {b} and count on {a}: that lands on {=a+b}. So {a} + {b} = {=a+b}.

pool.prompt: {a} + 6 + {=10-a}. Find two numbers that make 10 first. What is the total?
pool.explain: {a} + {=10-a} = 10, and 10 + 6 = 16. Adding in a different order gives the same total, 16.

pool.prompt: A domino has 4 dots on one side and 6 on the other. You turn it round. How many dots are there now?
pool.hint: Turning the domino round does not add or take away any dots.
pool.explain: There are still 10 dots. 4 + 6 = 10 and 6 + 4 = 10. 46 puts the digits side by side.

pool.prompt: Which one does NOT give the same answer as 7 + 2?
pool.explain: 7 − 2 is a take-away and makes 5, not 9. 2 + 7 is the turnaround, and 1 + 8 also makes 9.

pool.prompt: Leo works out 2 + 8 by starting on 2 and counting on 8. What is a quicker way?
pool.hint: You can add in any order. Which number is bigger?
pool.explain: Start on 8 and count on 2: 9, 10. Only 2 hops instead of 8, and the answer is still 10.

pool.prompt: Mia says, 'I know 5 + 9 = 14, but I need to work out 9 + 5 again.' What is true?
choices: 9 + 5 is 14 too, the same numbers turned round
pool.hint: Did either number change when the sum was turned round?
pool.explain: 9 + 5 = 14, because it uses the same two numbers. She does not need to work it out again.

pool.prompt: Sam has 3 stickers. He says he can give away 5 because 5 − 3 = 2. What is wrong?
choices: He cannot take 5 away from 3, so take-away does not turn round
pool.hint: Count out 3 stickers. Can you give 5 of them away?
pool.explain: He runs out after 3. 5 − 3 = 2 is true, but 3 − 5 is not the same, because take-away does not turn round.
